profile.name: Mervin Tabernero
profile.tagline: Transitioning from healthcare IT into SOC operations, focused on threat detection and Azure security.

alerts.whatTriggered: A process (PID 1864, masquerading as svchost.exe) opened a handle to lsass.exe (PID 840) and performed 1456 reads of process memory. This behavior is the exact definition of Defender's "Sensitive Credential Memory Detection (T1003.001 -LSASS Memory) is built to catch.
alerts.whyTriggered: The LSASS holds cached credentials, NTLM hashes, and Kerberos tickets in memory. Any non-system process reading its memory space is treated as high confidence credential-theft indicator, especially when accompanied by  a masquerading binary and a known credential-theft tool DLL loads.
alerts.whatHappened:
At 11:03:02 PM SOCSIM\dave.brown authenticated via a Network logon with domain Admin rights - the point at which the account was already compromised. At the same time, a svchost.exe process was spawned remotely via WMI, sourced from SOCSIM-SRV01 (172.31.6.185).
At 11:03:49 PM, a malicious file name svchost.exe was pushed to the DC via $$ administrative share (SMB) from 172.31.6.185 and  executed from C:\WIndows\Temp\ -- not the legitimate System32 location. It ran with the command line:
svchost.exe privilege::debug sekurlsa::logonpasswords exit
This is a well known Mimikatz CLi syntax: privilege:: debug elevates the the SeDebugPrivilege required to touch LSASS, and sekurlsa::logonpasswords is Mimikatz's core credential dumping module.
Immediately after the execution, the process loaded cryptdll.dll, samlib.dll, WinSCard.dll, and hid.dll in sequence -- the signature DLL -loading fingerprint of Mimikatz. It then opened a handle to the lsass.exe and, at 11:05:57 PM read its process memory (1456 reads/65402258 bytes copied).
Defender detected and quarantined the dropped file (EUS:Win32/CustomEnterpriseBlock) as a remediation -- but this remediation occured after the process had already executed  and begun reading LSASS memory (11:06:36PM), not before.
alerts.evidence:
[1864] svchost.exe  — Path: C:\Windows\Temp\svchost.exe (masquerade — real svchost = System32)
Command line: privilege::debug sekurlsa::logonpasswords exit
SHA1: e3b6ea8c46fa831cec6f235a5cf48b38a4ae8d69 (mimikatz.exe hash)
Integrity level: High | User: SOCSIM\dave.brown (real svchost = SYSTEM/System integrity)
Source device: SOCSIM-SRV01 / 172.31.6.185, delivered via C$ admin share
lsass.exe read: 1,456 reads, 6,402,256 bytes copied
Defender remediation: EUS:Win32/CustomEnterpriseBlock — quarantined post-execution
alerts.verdictJustification: Multiple indicators confirm malicious credential-theft activity: (1) a binary masquerading as a legitimate svchost.exe running from a non-standard location with elevated permission under a standard user account., (2) literal Mimikatz command line sysntax, (3) the signature Mimikatz DLL-loading pattern, (4) delivery via lateral movement over WMI/SMB admin shares from an internal host, (5) a Domain Admin account authenticating and conducting hands-on-keyboard activity, and (6) Defender's own correlation of the alert into a High-Severity, 19/23 aleet incident titled "Hands-on keyboard attack was launched from a compromised account".
investigationSteps: Opened the Alert "Sensitive credential memory read" in Defender and reviewed the alert story/Process Tree
Noted the affected host was a Domain COntroller (socsim-dc) and the account was SOCSIdave.brown -- classfied as high risk given the machine involved is a Domain controller.
Checked the linked incident('Hands-on keyboard attack was launched from a compromise account') to understand the broader attack chain rather than viewing the alert in isolation.
Walked the process tree chronologically: identified the 11:03:02:PM Domain Admin network logon and WMI-based remote process creation.
Pulled the raw process/event detaisl for PID 1864 and confirmed the path (C:\Windows\Temp\ - not system32), the command line, and the SHA1/creation time mismatch indicating a pre-staged tool.
Review the loaded - files( crypt.dll, samlib.dll, WinSCard.dll, hid.dll) abd recognized the Mimikatz DLL fingerprint.
Confirmed the handle-open, and memory-read events  against lsass.exe (PID840), noting the byte count and read count as evidence of a completed dump, not just an attempt.
Checked Defender's remediation status and confirmed the file was quarantined, but onluy after the credential-read activity already occured.
Mapped all the observed behavior to the MITRE ATT&CK techniques for the write-up
alerts.containment:
Force and immediate credential reset for SOCSIM\dave.brown and treat the account as fully compromised, not just the endpoint.
Isolate soc-sim and SOCSIM_SRV01 (172.31.6.185) pending full forensic review.
Audit all activities ferformed under dave.brown's Domain Admin sessions.
Revoew SOCSIM-SRV01 for how it was compromised.
Hunt across the environment for the same file hash (e3b6ea8c46fa831cec6f235a5cf48b38a4ae8d69) or the same cmdline pattern (sekurlsa::logonpasswords) on other hosts.
alerts.lessonsLearned:
Detection worked but the remediation happened only after Mimikatz had already loaded.
The path mismatch (Temp VS System32) was the single fastest tell that this was not a legitimate svchost.exe -- worth remembering to check process image path first.
Remember to chekc for a linked incident before writng up any individual alert.
This was a good first exposure to reading Mimikatz CLI syntax and associated DLLs -- worth commiting to memory as fast-recognition patterns for future alerts.
